name: Mongolia
summary_text: Mongolia is workable for trans visitors. Same-sex activity was decriminalised in 1993, discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited, and SOGI was added to the hate-crime provisions of the Criminal Code in 2015. Legal gender recognition exists via a medicalised process, and Ulaanbaatar has an organised community (LGBT Centre) that successfully lobbied for these protections. Counterweights: protections are fragmented (no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering all areas), the LGBT Centre has documented periods of elevated hate speech and assaults — including attacks on its own staff — and social acceptance outside the capital is low. There are no bathroom laws, no border/document friction for foreign passports, and no police targeting pattern; the realistic risk is street harassment if visibly trans, particularly at night and outside central Ulaanbaatar.

sources.title: Mongolia | Outright International
sources.claim_summary: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): notable progress since decriminalisation in 1993 - discrimination based on SOGI prohibited, but no comprehensive anti-discrimination law (protections fragmented); marriage equality constitutionally prohibited; legal gender recognition possible but requires medical intervention (not self-determination); hate-crime and non-discrimination provisions exist in penal and labour codes but enforcement is inconsistent.
ILGA World Database jurisdiction page for Mongolia: documents LGBTI-related legal frameworks — status of same-sex conduct (legal since 2002), discrimination protections and gender-recognition data.
ADB publication on the legal status of sexual and gender minorities in Asia and the Pacific - regional comparative overview including Mongolia.

sources.title: Mongolian Pride: LGBTQ Activism In One Developing Country – The Establishment
sources.claim_summary: The Establishment (Aug 2018): 'Mongolian Pride: LGBTQ Activism In One Developing Country' by Aubrey Menarndt - profiles Nyamdorj Anaraa, who came out three times (as a lesbian, then a trans man, then a gay trans man); LGBTQ activists leveraging political transition to create progressive change.

sources.title: Charges in Mongolia LGBT attack hint at changing attitudes | LGBTQ News | Al Jazeera
sources.claim_summary: Al Jazeera (Oct 2019): 'Charges in Mongolia LGBT attack hint at changing attitudes' - the far-right group Bosoo Khukh Mongol lured a trans sex worker into a hotel room with a TV station, threatened her and aired the video with commentary accusing LGBT people of paedophilia; charges were brought and investigated as a hate crime - a first; 2017 law changes added hate-crime protections and police training.

sources.title: Over 80 Nations Support Statement at Human Rights Council on LGBT Rights - U.S. Mission to International Organizations in Geneva
sources.claim_summary: US Mission in Geneva (March 2011): post on LGBT rights in the UN context - US diplomatic advocacy for SOGI rights at the Human Rights Council, relevant to Mongolia's international human-rights environment.

GlobalGayz Mongolia report: homosexuality has 'virtually no presence, no venues and no activism'; no laws specifically against homosexuality but 'satisfaction of immoral sexual needs' may still be illegal; a 2008 report described two organisations holding monthly parties for hundreds of members, 'all very furtive'.
